newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-BRITISH LIONS SPONSORED FOR FIRST TIME.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-BRITISH LIONS SPONSORED FOR FIRST TIME.

text.p: For the first time in their history, the British Lions will bear a sponsor's name on their jerseys during their 13 match tour of South Africa which begins in May.

The insurance company Scottish Provident is to invest 400,000 pounds sterling ($665,000) in the tour for which their name will feature on the traditional red playing jerseys, newly emblazoned with white stripes down the arms, as well as on leisure and training gear.

However, neither tour manager Fran Cotton nor Ray Williams, chairman of the Home Unions tours committee, would put a figure this week on how much would be going directly to the 35 players who will represent the first professional Lions side since the original tour to South Africa in 1910.

"We can't give figures at the moment because they are not firmly in place but they will be paid the same, a sum which I think even they might think is adequate." Williams told a news conference on Tuesday.
"There will be no sliding scale, they will all be paid precisely the same no matter how many matches or test matches they play."

The figure is expected to be around 15,000 pounds ($25,000) a man but Cotton, who was a member of three Lions sides including the 1974 team who beat the Springboks 3-0, was quick to play down the financial aspect of the tour.
"I think I can safely say that money is not the number one priority for the players. To play for the Lions is the pinnacle for any player, you cannot buy that," he said.
"We regard this as the flagship of northern hemisphere rugby going down there and only single-mindedness and hard work will bring about a test victory."

The tour is expected to cost in the region of one million pounds ($1,600,000) with the extra revenue coming from alternate sponsors and the South African Rugby Football Union whose input, although not finalised, was described by Williams as substantial.
"They have been very positive about making a significant contribution," he said.

At the news conference held at the South African High Commission there were understandably few clues as to the make-up of the tour party although Cotton's comment that he was encouraged by the return to action of Scotland captain Rob Wainwright should shorten the odds on the Lions' leadership.

Coach Ian McGeechan said he already had a few of the test side in his mind but stressed that although the Five Nations was a key factor in the selection process, players might be drawn from outside the competition.

"I want free thinkers," he said. " I want players who are positive, won't stay in their shells and will make decisions. From one to 15 I want rugby players who will play flexible and dynamic rugby with a hard mental edge."
Cotton did say the selectors would be meeting on February 9 and announcing a preliminary squad of 60 players which will meet for the first time on February 23.
The selection process, though, for the three-test tour will not be completed until early April with the tourists facing their first game in Port Elizabeth on May 24.
